title: Meet your metrics
subtitle: Turn a stream of measurements into a story.

lessons.title: A metric is a measurement with context
lessons.body: Imagine checking the number of active users every 30 seconds. Each observation is a sample: a timestamp and a value. Prometheus stores those samples as time series. A metric name describes what is measured; labels describe which service, instance, or environment produced it. Changing a label value creates a different series. The unit matters: 250 milliseconds is not 250 seconds.
lessons.sql_connection: A SQL table can hold timestamp, metric, service, instance, and value columns. Repeated rows over time represent observations. A Prometheus series is identified by its metric name and complete label set, rather than by a primary-key column.

lessons.title: Read one moment, then read the story
lessons.body: An instant query evaluates an expression at one timestamp. A range query evaluates that expression again at evenly spaced times. The same expression can therefore produce a current table or a time-series chart. Our lab uses fixed synthetic timestamps, so everyone can reproduce the same results. Begin with app_active_sessions and inspect the service and instance labels.
lessons.sql_connection: The snapshot table contains samples exactly at the lab's selected evaluation time. The samples table contains history. SELECT * FROM samples is not automatically equivalent to a PromQL instant selector: real Prometheus also applies lookback and staleness rules.

takeaways: A sample is a timestamp plus a value.
A series is identified by metric name and all its labels.
Always ask what unit a value uses.
pitfalls: Summing every historical SQL row when you meant one instant.
Assuming two differently labeled series are the same measurement.
equivalence: Equivalent on this fixture snapshot because a sample exists at the evaluation timestamp. Historical SQL rows need explicit time selection.
lab: Return every active-session series at the evaluation time.
lab_hint: A metric name by itself selects its series.

animation.title: Watch samples become a time series
steps: One measurement arrives: a timestamp and value.
Another sample arrives for the same label set.
The samples form a time series.
A second instance creates a separate series.
An instant query selects one value per series.
animation.sql: Rows over time → one labeled series

questions.prompt: What identifies a Prometheus time series?
options: Metric name and complete label set
questions.explanation: Two series can have the same value and timestamp. Metric name plus labels distinguish them.

questions.prompt: What does a sample contain?
questions.explanation: A sample records a value at a specific time; the surrounding series supplies the labels.

questions.prompt: Changing instance='a' to instance='b' creates…
questions.explanation: The full label set is part of series identity.

questions.prompt: What does an instant query evaluate?
questions.explanation: The evaluation happens at one instant, although functions can look backward over a window.

questions.prompt: Why display units next to a metric?
questions.explanation: Seconds, bytes, and ratios need different interpretations.

questions.prompt: A range query is conceptually…
options: An instant evaluation repeated at steps
questions.explanation: A range query repeats evaluation across timestamps. A range vector is a different concept.

questions.prompt: Which SQL table in this app represents a single lab instant?
questions.explanation: snapshot selects only rows at the chosen fixture evaluation time.

title: Find the signal
subtitle: Select exactly the series you want.

lessons.title: Metric selectors and label matchers
lessons.body: Start with a metric, then add label matchers inside braces. up{service="api"} selects only API targets. Multiple matchers are combined with AND. The operators = and != match exact values; =~ and !~ use regular expressions. Prometheus regex matchers are anchored, so api matches the complete label value, while .*api.* means contains api.
lessons.sql_connection: A label filter resembles WHERE service = 'api'. Several matchers resemble predicates joined by AND. SQL regex functions differ by dialect, so the SQL lab uses explicit full-match semantics when comparing regex behavior.

lessons.title: Missing labels are not SQL NULL
lessons.body: A matcher that matches an empty label value can also match a series where that label is absent. That matters for environment="" and negative matchers. Prefer explicit selectors when the intent is to require a label. A selector without a metric name must include at least one matcher that does not match the empty string.
lessons.sql_connection: SQL uses three-valued NULL logic. A missing Prometheus label should not be casually mapped to WHERE label IS NULL. Our fixture uses empty strings for absent dimensions; real SQL schemas may choose NULL instead.

takeaways: Matchers inside braces narrow the series set.
Regex matchers are fully anchored.
Absent labels need explicit consideration.
pitfalls: Using SQL LIKE syntax inside a PromQL selector.
Assuming a negative matcher guarantees the label exists.
equivalence: Equivalent for these explicit labels and exact-timestamp fixtures. Missing-label and SQL NULL behavior differ.
lab: Select the availability series for the API service only.
lab_hint: Use up with a service="api" matcher.

animation.title: See label filters select a signal
steps: Start with four labeled series.
Choose the service label.
Compare each label to api.
Keep matching API series.
SQL WHERE selects the corresponding rows.

questions.prompt: Which selects API availability?
questions.explanation: PromQL label matchers belong inside braces after the metric name.

questions.prompt: Multiple matchers inside braces use…
questions.explanation: A series must satisfy every matcher.

questions.prompt: What does service=~"api" match?
questions.explanation: Prometheus regex matches are fully anchored.

questions.prompt: Which operator means regex does not match?
questions.explanation: != is exact inequality; !~ negates the regex matcher.

questions.prompt: A matcher service="" can match…
questions.explanation: Matchers matching empty values also match series without that label.

questions.prompt: What is the closest SQL idea to a label matcher?
questions.explanation: Both narrow the selected data using predicates.

questions.prompt: Which metric-free selector is valid?
questions.explanation: A metric-free selector needs a matcher that excludes an empty string. .+ requires a nonempty value.

title: Know your metric
subtitle: Counters climb. Gauges move. Types shape the query.

lessons.title: Counters and gauges answer different questions
lessons.body: A counter accumulates events and normally increases until its process restarts. http_requests_total answers how many requests have accumulated, not requests per second. A gauge measures a current quantity such as active sessions or queue depth, and can move up or down. Naming conventions help, but applying rate() to an ordinary float gauge can still run and produce a misleading answer.
lessons.sql_connection: A counter resembles a running cumulative total stored in each row. A gauge resembles a current balance. The column type DOUBLE does not express that distinction, so a SQL analyst must understand the measurement too.

lessons.title: Instant vectors and range vectors
lessons.body: app_active_sessions is an instant-vector selector. queue_depth[5m] selects a range of samples per series, with a left-open and right-closed interval. Functions such as avg_over_time consume range vectors and return instant vectors. A range query and a range-vector selector are not interchangeable: one describes how the API evaluates an expression, the other describes a value inside the expression.
lessons.sql_connection: A range-vector selector resembles grouping time-filtered rows by series. The analogous filter is timestamp > evaluation_time - 300 AND timestamp <= evaluation_time. Aggregation across rows must still respect each series identity.

takeaways: Counters accumulate events; gauges measure current quantities.
A range vector contains multiple samples per series.
Range queries and range vectors are different.
pitfalls: Reading a counter's absolute value as throughput.
Using rate() on a gauge just because the expression parses.
equivalence: An exact comparison of a gauge snapshot; it is not a rate calculation.
lab: Select the active-session gauge for the web service.
lab_hint: Use the active-session metric, then select web.

animation.title: Counter or gauge? Watch the difference
steps: A counter starts accumulating events.
More events increase the counter.
A restart resets the counter.
A gauge can rise or fall normally.
Choose a calculation that fits the metric type.

questions.prompt: Which is naturally a gauge?
questions.explanation: Queue depth can increase and decrease without a process reset.

questions.prompt: A counter drops to zero. What may have happened?
questions.explanation: Counters can reset when their process restarts; rate functions account for this.

questions.prompt: Which expression returns a range vector?
questions.explanation: The [5m] selector gathers a range of samples for each selected series.

questions.prompt: Does a valid rate(gauge[5m]) guarantee a meaningful result?
options: No, the metric type still matters
questions.explanation: Prometheus float samples do not enforce counter versus gauge flavor.

questions.prompt: What is the usual counter name suffix?
questions.explanation: _total is a naming convention for cumulative counters.

questions.prompt: What is the boundary of a [5m] range selector?
questions.explanation: A sample exactly five minutes before evaluation is excluded.

questions.prompt: A range query always returns the same thing as metric[5m].
questions.explanation: A range query repeats evaluation; metric[5m] is a range-vector expression.

title: Group the story
subtitle: Roll instances up into meaningful service views.

lessons.title: Aggregate across series at one moment
lessons.body: sum by (service) (app_active_sessions) adds the current values of instances within each service. The result retains service and drops other grouping dimensions. avg, min, max, and count answer different questions. count counts series, not the events represented by a counter. without(instance) removes just that label, leaving every other label to define groups.
lessons.sql_connection: GROUP BY service with SUM(value) is the closest SQL counterpart on a snapshot. SQL COUNT(*) counts rows; PromQL count() counts selected series. Summing a counter snapshot gives an accumulated total, not throughput.

lessons.title: Grouping changes the output labels
lessons.body: Think of labels as the keys of an intermediate result. After sum by(service), an instance label is gone, so subsequent matching must use the labels that remain. sum without(instance) can preserve unexpected dimensions such as environment. topk picks the highest values; over a range query, the winning series can change at each evaluation timestamp.
lessons.sql_connection: A SQL GROUP BY changes result granularity. Joining that grouped result to a detailed table requires a deliberate relationship. ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT k resembles topk at a single evaluation time.

takeaways: by lists labels to keep.
without lists labels to remove.
count counts series, not counter events.
pitfalls: Aggregating every historical sample instead of a snapshot.
Forgetting which labels survive an aggregation.
sql:
SELECT service, SUM(value) AS value
FROM snapshot
WHERE metric = 'app_active_sessions'
GROUP BY service;
equivalence: Equivalent on the fixture snapshot, including one output row/series per service.
lab: Return the total active sessions for each service.
lab_hint: Sum the gauge and keep the service label.

animation.title: Watch instances roll into service totals
steps: Each instance begins as a separate series.
Read the service label on each series.
Move API instances into one group.
Move web instances into another group.
Add within each group; preserve only service.

questions.prompt: What does by(service) preserve?
questions.explanation: by explicitly names the labels that remain as grouping keys.

questions.prompt: What does without(instance) remove?
questions.explanation: All other labels can still define separate groups.

questions.prompt: count(http_requests_total) counts…
questions.explanation: count counts vector elements. Counter values represent the events.

questions.prompt: Which SQL idea matches sum by(service)?
questions.explanation: Both aggregate at service granularity.

questions.prompt: After sum by(service), can you assume instance is present?
questions.explanation: The aggregation has discarded the instance dimension.

questions.prompt: Which finds the largest three current gauge values?
questions.explanation: topk selects vector elements with the highest values at that evaluation time.

questions.prompt: Does sum(counter) give requests per second?
questions.explanation: Use rate on each counter before aggregation for throughput.

title: Think in rates
subtitle: Turn cumulative counters into useful throughput.

lessons.title: Rate measures change per second
lessons.body: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) estimates the average per-second increase over five minutes. It adjusts for counter resets and extrapolates to the range boundaries. increase() expresses the estimated increase over the whole window, so it need not be an integer. irate() uses the last two samples and is more sensitive to short-lived changes; rate() is generally better for stable alert expressions.
lessons.sql_connection: SQL LAG can compare consecutive counter samples. Reset-aware differences are a useful analogy, but simple endpoint subtraction does not reproduce Prometheus extrapolation or sparse-sample handling. The paired SQL calculates a sample-based estimate and is deliberately labeled as such.

lessons.title: Rate first, then aggregate
lessons.body: A counter reset belongs to one original series. If you first sum instances, one reset can be hidden by another instance's increase. Calculate rate for each series before sum by(service). Choose a window long enough to contain several scrapes, and remember that a five-minute rate evaluated now looks backward rather than predicting the next five minutes.
lessons.sql_connection: Partition a SQL LAG window by the complete counter identity before grouping by service. Otherwise you subtract values from unrelated instances or status codes. The order of transformations is part of correctness.

takeaways: rate returns events per second.
increase estimates the change across the window.
Calculate rate before aggregation to detect per-series resets.
pitfalls: Treating rate() as an average of counter values.
Expecting a simple SQL delta to match Prometheus exactly.
sql:
WITH deltas AS (
  SELECT service, instance, status, value,
    LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY service, instance, status ORDER BY timestamp) AS prev
  FROM samples
  WHERE metric = 'http_requests_total'
    AND timestamp BETWEEN (SELECT MAX(timestamp)-300 FROM snapshot)
                      AND (SELECT MAX(timestamp) FROM snapshot)
)
SELECT service,
  SUM(CASE WHEN value >= prev THEN value-prev ELSE value END) / 300 AS sample_rate
FROM deltas WHERE prev IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY service;
equivalence: Conceptual, sample-based SQL estimate. Prometheus also handles resets and extrapolation; exact equality is not promised.
lab: Return average requests per second for each service over five minutes.
lab_hint: Apply rate to each counter series, then sum by service.

animation.title: A counter reset should not mean negative traffic
steps: A counter accumulates requests.
Compare neighboring samples.
A restart drops the counter.
Detect the reset before grouping.
Divide the corrected change by elapsed time; Prometheus also extrapolates.
animation.sql: LAG + reset-aware deltas is an analogy, not exact rate()

questions.prompt: The unit of rate(requests_total[5m]) is…
questions.explanation: rate always returns a per-second average, regardless of window duration.

questions.prompt: Which order preserves reset detection?
questions.explanation: Resets must be detected within the original counter series.

questions.prompt: What does irate use?
questions.explanation: irate is sensitive to the most recent interval.

questions.prompt: Can increase() return a fractional value?
questions.explanation: The estimate includes extrapolation to window boundaries.

questions.prompt: A counter resets during a window. rate()…
questions.explanation: Prometheus interprets a decrease as a counter reset.

questions.prompt: Is SQL AVG(counter_value) equivalent to rate()?
questions.explanation: A mean of cumulative values is not a change per second.

questions.prompt: Why use several scrapes in a rate window?
options: To obtain a useful change estimate
questions.explanation: A rate needs multiple samples, and a broader window can smooth short-term fluctuations.

title: Build useful ratios
subtitle: Combine expressions into signals you can act on.

lessons.title: Numerators and denominators need matching labels
lessons.body: An error ratio divides the request rate for errors by the request rate for all requests. Aggregate both sides to the same service label set before dividing. The result is a fraction: 0.02 means 2%. Multiplying by 100 is a display choice. A denominator of zero can produce NaN or infinity, and a missing denominator series can remove the result entirely.
lessons.sql_connection: SQL uses grouped conditional sums or joins of aggregated subqueries. Use compatible grouping keys and understand NULLIF for zero denominators. A missing joined row, SQL NULL, and PromQL NaN or absent series are distinct states.

lessons.title: Filtering is different from returning a boolean
lessons.body: metric > 10 filters out elements whose values do not exceed 10 and keeps the original value of matches. metric > bool 10 instead returns 0 or 1 for matched elements. Set operators and, or, and unless operate on label-set membership, not the truthiness of sample values. An or expression can provide a fallback, but matching labels still determine which series survive.
lessons.sql_connection: WHERE value > 10 resembles filtering. CASE WHEN value > 10 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END resembles the bool modifier. EXISTS and anti-joins are useful analogies for set membership; SQL three-valued logic is not identical.

takeaways: Build ratios from compatible numerator and denominator labels.
Comparisons filter by default.
bool changes the returned values to zero or one.
pitfalls: Averaging per-instance error percentages instead of dividing summed rates.
Confusing an absent result with the numeric value zero.
sql:
SELECT service,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = '500' THEN value ELSE 0 END)
  / NULLIF(SUM(value), 0) AS cumulative_error_fraction
FROM snapshot
WHERE metric = 'http_requests_total'
GROUP BY service;
equivalence: This SQL shows conditional aggregation on cumulative totals. The PromQL expression measures a recent rate ratio; they are not generally equivalent.
lab: Calculate the five-minute error fraction for each service.
lab_hint: Divide summed error rates by summed total rates, with service on both sides.

animation.title: From traffic to an error fraction
steps: Count all requests in a window.
Identify the errors inside that total.
Keep numerator and denominator grouped alike.
Divide errors by total requests.
A fraction of 0.08 is an error rate of 8%.

questions.prompt: What does a ratio of 0.02 represent?
questions.explanation: Multiply a fraction by 100 to express it as a percentage.

questions.prompt: A comparison without bool usually…
options: Filters series and keeps matching values
questions.explanation: For example, a matching value of 12 remains 12 after > 10.

questions.prompt: What does > bool 10 return for a matched value of 12?
questions.explanation: bool changes the result to 1 when the comparison is true.

questions.prompt: How should service error ratios be combined?
options: Divide summed error rates by summed total rates
questions.explanation: This correctly weights instances by traffic.

questions.prompt: What does unless primarily compare?
questions.explanation: It keeps left-side elements without a matching right-side element.

questions.prompt: A missing denominator series is always equivalent to zero.
questions.explanation: Missing matching elements can remove the result; zero is a present numeric sample.

questions.prompt: Why group both ratio operands the same way?
questions.explanation: Binary vector arithmetic requires matching elements.

title: Travel through time
subtitle: Move windows, compare history, and compose time calculations.

lessons.title: A window moves with evaluation time
lessons.body: avg_over_time(queue_depth[5m]) averages the available samples of each series in the last five minutes. It does not first average across instances. Each sample has equal weight, even with uneven spacing. offset shifts the selector into the past; @ pins it to a timestamp. A range query repeatedly evaluates the expression, causing its lookback window to slide.
lessons.sql_connection: Filter timestamped rows to a window, then GROUP BY the series identity. A SQL ROWS frame counts rows; a time interval counts time. SQL time-weighted averages require extra logic and are not the same as avg_over_time.

lessons.title: Subqueries create a history of an expression
lessons.body: A subquery such as rate(http_requests_total[5m])[10m:1m] evaluates a rate expression at a one-minute resolution over ten minutes. max_over_time can then summarize those intermediate rates. Subqueries are powerful but increase work. Choose a useful resolution and limit the time span instead of calculating far more samples than the lesson needs.
lessons.sql_connection: A CTE can compute intermediate values, and a second query can aggregate them. To match a PromQL subquery, SQL also needs an explicit evaluation-time grid. A CTE alone does not reproduce the timing semantics.

takeaways: Time-window functions operate within each series.
offset shifts time; @ pins time.
Subquery resolution controls intermediate evaluation spacing.
pitfalls: Confusing a SQL ROWS window with a time interval.
Assuming avg_over_time is weighted by the duration between samples.
sql:
SELECT service, instance, environment, AVG(value) AS value
FROM samples
WHERE metric = 'queue_depth'
  AND timestamp > (SELECT MAX(timestamp)-300 FROM snapshot)
  AND timestamp <= (SELECT MAX(timestamp) FROM snapshot)
GROUP BY service, instance, environment;
equivalence: Equivalent sample averaging on these regular float samples; the SQL interval matches PromQL's left-open, right-closed window.
lab: Return each queue's average depth over the last five minutes.
lab_hint: Use the time-window average function on a range vector.

animation.title: Slide a five-minute window through time
steps: Put samples on a timeline.
Place the window at evaluation time.
Move the evaluation time forward.
Old samples leave and new samples enter.
Average only the samples inside each series window.
animation.sql: timestamp > t - window AND timestamp <= t

questions.prompt: avg_over_time averages…
questions.explanation: Aggregation over time is different from aggregation across series.

questions.prompt: What does offset 1h do?
options: Reads the selector one hour earlier
questions.explanation: offset shifts the selector's reference time.

questions.prompt: What does @ pin?
questions.explanation: @ lets a selector use a specific timestamp.

questions.prompt: Are samples duration-weighted in avg_over_time?
questions.explanation: Irregular sampling can make a sample mean differ from a time-weighted average.

questions.prompt: What does :1m specify in a subquery?
questions.explanation: It spaces the subquery evaluations one minute apart.

questions.prompt: Does SQL ROWS BETWEEN 5 PRECEDING mean five minutes?
questions.explanation: The elapsed duration depends on how rows are spaced.

questions.prompt: What can increase subquery cost?
questions.explanation: More intermediate evaluation points mean more computation.

title: Make labels meet
subtitle: Understand vector matching through the lens of joins.

lessons.title: Vector arithmetic matches series by labels
lessons.body: When dividing two instant vectors, Prometheus finds matching elements using their labels. on(service) limits the matching key to service. ignoring(status) excludes status from the matching key. Unmatched elements disappear from arithmetic results. These rules explain many queries that return an empty result despite both inputs containing data.
lessons.sql_connection: An equijoin on service is a useful analogy. SQL may allow duplicate matches that multiply rows; PromQL arithmetic matching imposes uniqueness constraints. A query can fail instead of silently producing a many-to-many multiplication.

lessons.title: Enrich measurements with metadata
lessons.body: A service_info series can associate a service with a team. Multiply a service-level measurement by on(service) group_left(team) service_info to copy team into the result. The right side must be unique for the matching key. group_left identifies the left side as potentially having more elements; group_right is the reverse. The result still follows Prometheus's rules for which labels and metric names remain.
lessons.sql_connection: This resembles joining measurements to a unique dimension table. Check the uniqueness of the dimension key before the join. group_left does not mean a SQL LEFT OUTER JOIN: unmatched left series can still disappear.

takeaways: on names matching keys; ignoring removes keys from matching.
The one side must be unique.
group_left is not a SQL left outer join.
pitfalls: Using group_left to try to allow unrestricted many-to-many arithmetic.
Assuming all unmatched measurements will be preserved.
sql:
WITH totals AS (
 SELECT service, SUM(value) AS value FROM snapshot
 WHERE metric = 'app_active_sessions' GROUP BY service
)
SELECT t.service, i.team, t.value
FROM totals t JOIN snapshot i ON t.service = i.service
WHERE i.metric = 'service_info';
equivalence: Equivalent for this fixture's unique service_info series with value 1. A group_left operation is not a general SQL LEFT JOIN.
lab: Return total active sessions per service, enriched with the owning team.
lab_hint: First aggregate sessions by service, then match service_info and copy team.

animation.title: Join by the labels that actually match
steps: Measurements and metadata start separately.
Choose service as the matching key.
Connect matching API elements.
Connect matching web elements.
Copy team from the unique metadata side.
animation.sql: Join on a unique dimension key; unmatched series disappear

questions.prompt: What does on(service) specify?
questions.explanation: Only the listed labels are used to match elements.

questions.prompt: What does ignoring(status) do?
options: Excludes status from the matching key
questions.explanation: The label is ignored for matching, not used as a filter.

questions.prompt: For many-to-one group_left arithmetic, which side must be unique?
questions.explanation: The right side is the one side for the selected matching key.

questions.prompt: Is group_left a SQL LEFT OUTER JOIN?
questions.explanation: Unmatched left series are not automatically retained.

questions.prompt: Unmatched elements in vector division…
questions.explanation: Arithmetic operations need a matching counterpart.

questions.prompt: What does group_left(team) copy?
options: The team label from the one side
questions.explanation: The label list names additional labels to include from the one side.

questions.prompt: Why validate service_info uniqueness?
questions.explanation: Multiple right-side elements with the same match key can make arithmetic matching invalid.

title: Read the distribution
subtitle: Understand what your latency percentile really says.

lessons.title: Classic histograms store cumulative buckets
lessons.body: A classic histogram exposes _bucket, _count, and _sum series. Each le label is an inclusive upper bound, and larger buckets also include observations counted in smaller buckets. To estimate service p95 latency, first rate the bucket counters, then aggregate by service and le, then apply histogram_quantile(0.95, ...). Keep le during aggregation because it defines the bucket boundaries.
lessons.sql_connection: A table of raw request durations can calculate a percentile directly. A table of cumulative bucket counts has already lost information and needs interpolation. SQL percentile_cont over bucket counts is not a latency percentile.

lessons.title: Percentiles are estimates, and summaries differ
lessons.body: A histogram quantile is estimated from the bucket distribution. Accuracy depends on bucket layout and the observations' location within buckets. Native histograms encode a distribution in a sample and use different query shapes; classic _bucket syntax is not universal. Summaries may expose precomputed quantiles, which cannot generally be averaged across instances to get the fleet percentile.
lessons.sql_connection: Percentiles of raw rows and percentiles inferred from aggregated buckets answer related questions with different available information. A weighted average of two p95 values is not the combined p95. Merge distributions before estimating a combined quantile.

takeaways: Classic buckets are cumulative.
Keep le when aggregating classic histogram buckets.
Never average instance p95 values to get a service p95.
pitfalls: Dropping le before histogram_quantile.
Running a percentile function over bucket counts as if they were raw durations.
sql:
SELECT service, le, SUM(value) AS cumulative_bucket_count
FROM snapshot
WHERE metric = 'http_request_duration_seconds_bucket'
GROUP BY service, le;
equivalence: This SQL exposes the bucket representation for inspection. It does not compute p95; raw-duration percentiles and bucket interpolation are different operations.
lab: Estimate p95 request duration per service from the classic histogram.
lab_hint: Rate each bucket counter, keep service and le during aggregation, then estimate the 0.95 quantile.

animation.title: Watch cumulative buckets fill up
steps: Requests arrive with different durations.
An observation increments every bucket whose bound contains it.
Larger buckets accumulate the smaller buckets too.
Find where 95% of observations fall.
Estimate inside the bucket; this is not an exact raw-sample percentile.
animation.sql: Raw durations and bucket counts contain different information

questions.prompt: What does le mean in a classic histogram?
options: Less than or equal upper bound
questions.explanation: A bucket counts observations at or below its le boundary.

questions.prompt: Classic histogram buckets are…
questions.explanation: An observation appears in every bucket whose upper bound includes it.

questions.prompt: Which label must survive classic bucket aggregation?
questions.explanation: histogram_quantile needs bucket boundaries.

questions.prompt: What should happen before summing bucket counters?
questions.explanation: Bucket counters can reset independently, so calculate rate first.

questions.prompt: Does averaging instance p95 values produce the service p95?
questions.explanation: Merge distributions; averages of quantiles do not generally preserve percentiles.

questions.prompt: histogram_quantile returns…
options: An exact median for all data
questions.explanation: It interpolates from bucket information.

questions.prompt: Native histograms always require an _bucket metric and le.
questions.explanation: Native histograms store distributions in samples and have different query shapes.

title: Build reliable signals
subtitle: Handle missing data, expensive queries, and alert state.

lessons.title: Missing is different from healthy
lessons.body: up == 0 finds targets that are present and report failure. It does not automatically detect a series that has disappeared. absent() and absent_over_time() can help detect missing expected data, but a global absent query cannot invent the names of all expected instances. Use an inventory or an explicit target selector when identity matters. Stale series disappear from instant-vector selection according to Prometheus rules.
lessons.sql_connection: A failed row can be selected with WHERE value = 0. A missing row may need a LEFT JOIN from an inventory and an IS NULL check. Coalescing every missing measurement to zero can hide collection failures.

lessons.title: Recording and alerting rules have state
lessons.body: A recording rule evaluates an expression periodically and stores the result as another series. An alert rule evaluates a condition; a for duration requires that condition to remain active before firing. The PromQL [5m] calculation window and an alert's for: 5m are separate concepts. High-cardinality labels such as request_id multiply series and make storage and queries more expensive.
lessons.sql_connection: A recording rule resembles a periodically maintained derived table, but its evaluation schedule matters. A SQL view is often computed on demand. An alert's pending-to-firing transition needs state across evaluations, not just one WHERE clause.

takeaways: No result is not automatically zero or healthy.
An alert hold duration is separate from a query window.
Keep unbounded values out of metric labels.
pitfalls: Using up == 0 as the only check for disappeared targets.
Treating a recording rule exactly like an on-demand SQL view.
sql:
SELECT service, COUNT(*) AS value
FROM snapshot
WHERE metric = 'up' AND value = 0
GROUP BY service;
equivalence: Equivalent for present targets in the selected snapshot. A disappeared target requires an expected-target inventory.
lab: Count the currently failing, present targets for each service. Healthy services should be absent.
lab_hint: Filter up to failed targets, then count the matching series by service.

animation.title: From missing samples to a firing alert
steps: A present healthy target reports up = 1.
A failed scrape reports up = 0.
A disappeared series is absent, not numeric zero.
An alert condition becomes pending.
It fires only after the condition persists for its hold duration.
animation.sql: Failed rows ≠ missing rows; alert state persists over time

questions.prompt: Does up == 0 find every disappeared target?
questions.explanation: It selects present series with value zero. Missing expected series need additional logic.

questions.prompt: What is absent() useful for?
questions.explanation: It indicates absence; it does not reconstruct an arbitrary missing inventory.

questions.prompt: What does an alert for duration mean?
options: The expression stays active before firing
questions.explanation: The alert remains pending while the condition is active for the required period.

questions.prompt: Which label is a cardinality concern?
questions.explanation: Unbounded identifiers create many distinct series.

questions.prompt: What does a recording rule do?
questions.explanation: It materializes evaluated results as new time series on a schedule.

questions.prompt: How do you count present failed targets?
questions.explanation: Filtering retains zero values; summing them gives zero. Counting the selected series gives the number of failures.

questions.prompt: A query window of [5m] and for: 5m mean the same thing.

title: Own the incident
subtitle: Bring everything together and earn PromQL Hero.

lessons.title: Investigate the service, not just one chart
lessons.body: An incident investigation combines traffic, errors, latency, and availability. First confirm that the service is receiving traffic and data is fresh. Then compare error fractions and latency distributions. A slow request and a failed request are different events. In the incident fixture, traffic and error fraction rise, latency shifts, and one web target reports up = 0. Use each signal to test a specific hypothesis.
lessons.sql_connection: An analytical investigation joins multiple measures at compatible granularity and time boundaries. A dashboard assembled from individually plausible queries can still mislead if each panel uses a different population or denominator.

lessons.title: Connect an SLI to an SLO
lessons.body: An SLI measures a defined outcome such as successful eligible requests divided by all eligible requests. An SLO specifies a target over a compliance window. For a 99.9% success target, the allowed error fraction is 0.001. A short-window error fraction of 0.01 represents 10 times that allowed fraction, but does not by itself prove the entire compliance window has failed. Real burn-rate alerting usually considers multiple windows and minimum traffic.
lessons.sql_connection: A SQL report can calculate an SLI from eligible event rows. It must use the same definition, time range, and exclusions as the monitoring query. A five-minute diagnostic is not a full monthly SLO report.

takeaways: Validate traffic, errors, latency, and availability together.
Make numerator, denominator, and eligibility explicit.
Distinguish a short-window burn rate from a compliance-window result.
pitfalls: Declaring a monthly SLO breach from one five-minute sample.
Averaging percentages without traffic weighting.
sql:
SELECT service,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = '500' THEN value ELSE 0 END)
    / NULLIF(SUM(value), 0) AS cumulative_error_fraction
FROM snapshot WHERE metric = 'http_requests_total'
GROUP BY service
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN status = '500' THEN value ELSE 0 END)
    / NULLIF(SUM(value), 0) > 0.05;
equivalence: The SQL illustrates grouped threshold filtering on accumulated counts. The PromQL condition uses recent rates and can differ after resets or changing traffic.
lab: Find services whose five-minute error fraction exceeds 5%. Keep the error fraction as the value; healthy services must disappear. Your query must work in both normal traffic and the incident.
lab_hint: Build the service-level error fraction, then use > 0.05 without bool.

animation.title: Follow the evidence through an incident
steps: Normal traffic: availability is high and errors are low.
Traffic grows: check the denominator.
Errors rise: calculate a traffic-weighted fraction.
Latency shifts: inspect the histogram and p95.
Combine the evidence, then choose an actionable alert.

questions.prompt: A 99.9% success SLO allows what error fraction?
questions.explanation: 100% - 99.9% = 0.1%, which is the fraction 0.001.

questions.prompt: An error fraction of 0.01 against a 0.001 budget fraction has burn rate…
questions.explanation: Divide the observed error fraction by the allowed error fraction.

questions.prompt: Does a five-minute spike alone prove a monthly SLO breach?
questions.explanation: A compliance-window result requires the eligible data across that full window.

questions.prompt: Which should be checked before interpreting an error ratio?
questions.explanation: Low traffic and missing data can make ratios misleading.

questions.prompt: To keep actual fractions above 5%, use…
questions.explanation: A regular comparison filters and preserves the matching ratio values.

questions.prompt: Why investigate latency separately from errors?
questions.explanation: A service can meet success criteria while being unacceptably slow.

questions.prompt: What makes a useful alert?
options: A clear symptom and an actionable response
questions.explanation: Alerts should communicate a meaningful condition someone can act on.
